articles.title: 100 billion times smaller than atom, scientists explore 'zeptoverse'
articles.summary: Scientists have detected signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored, opening a new window into a mysterious world around 100 billion times
articles.body: Scientists have detected signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored, opening a new window into a mysterious world around 100 billion times smaller than an atom, which physicists have nicknamed the 'zeptoverse'. The finding could help researchers investigate unknown particles and forces that may hold clues to some of the universe's biggest mysteries, including dark matter.According to a report by BBC News, the research was led by scientists based at the University of Cambridge using data from the Large Hadron Collider's LHCb experiment at CERN, the European particle physics laboratory on the Swiss-French border.The research was conducted using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), a massive particle accelerator operated by CERN on the Swiss-French border. The machine smashes particles together at extremely high speeds, allowing scientists to study the smaller particles produced in these collisions.The researchers detected evidence of an extremely rare process involving a subatomic particle containing a beauty quark, which breaks down into two particles called muons. Beauty quarks exist for an extremely short period before decaying into other particles, making their behaviour difficult to study.The experiment allowed scientists to investigate particle interactions at a scale of around one zeptometre, or one-sextillionth of a metre.This is the scale that researchers have nicknamed the 'zeptoverse'. The finding marks an important step in exploring how matter behaves at distances far smaller than those previously accessible to experimental studies.Dr Harry Cliff, a physicist at the University of Cambridge who led the analysis of the data, described the finding as a significant step towards exploring the mysterious scale, saying, "We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse."He said the experiment had given researchers an opportunity to study the behaviour of possible new particles."And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff told BBC News.How the discovery could help unlock the mystery of dark matterDark matter is one of the biggest unsolved mysteries in modern physics. It is an invisible form of matter that does not emit, absorb or reflect light, making it impossible to observe directly through conventional telescopes. Scientists infer its existence from its gravitational effects on visible matter, including the movement of stars and galaxies. Despite its significant presence in the universe, researchers have not yet identified what it is made of.The latest research could offer another way to investigate this mystery. Scientists believe that undiscovered particles, which cannot always be produced or detected directly, could influence the behaviour of known subatomic particles. In particular, hypothetical particles could affect the rare decay of beauty mesons by contributing to the quantum processes involved in their breakdown.By studying these extremely rare interactions, researchers can look for deviations from the predictions of the Standard Model, the established theory of particle physics.Any unexplained differences could point towards new particles or forces that are not yet part of our understanding of the universe. Some theoretical models suggest that such particles could also be connected to dark matter.

articles.title: Every autumn, residents of Portugal’s tiny Corvo Island switch off public lights for five nights to help young seabirds find the ocean; the wider Azores rescue campaign has saved more than 30,000 fledglings since 2015
articles.summary: Imagine an entire island voluntarily turning off its lights, allowing the night sky to guide thousands of young birds towards the ocean.
articles.body: Imagine an entire island voluntarily turning off its lights, allowing the night sky to guide thousands of young birds towards the ocean. On Corvo, the smallest and northernmost island of Portugal’s Azores archipelago, darkness is not a sign of inactivity but an important conservation effort. Every autumn, residents come together to reduce artificial lighting, giving young seabirds a better chance of completing their first journey out to sea. What began as a small community-led rescue initiative has evolved into a wider conservation movement, demonstrating how simple changes in everyday life can make a significant difference to wildlife.A blackout with a purposeHome to approximately 450 residents, Corvo has been working to protect Cory’s shearwaters since 1991, when locals began noticing large numbers of young birds dying after leaving their nests. According to The Guardian, these seabirds spend around three months in their nests before attempting their first flight towards the Atlantic Ocean. They follow natural light and the night sky, but street and building light can confuse them and draw them toward populated areas.Disoriented birds often hit buildings or roads, making them easy prey for predators, vehicles, and dehydration. Residents started nighttime patrols to return stranded birds to the ocean.The initiative gained wider recognition in 1995, when the Azorean government launched SOS Cagarro, a campaign extending rescue efforts across all nine islands. The Portuguese Society for the Study of Birds (SPEA) subsequently became involved, helping strengthen conservation and public awareness programmes.Five nights of darknessThe island's approach has gradually expanded beyond rescuing stranded birds. According to SPEA, public lighting is switched off during particularly vulnerable periods in autumn, when young Cory's shearwaters leave their nests. The latest five-night initiative, organised between October 26 and 30, involves switching off public lights between 9pm and 4am.Residents and volunteers continue patrolling Vila do Corvo, the island's only settlement, looking for birds that have become disoriented. Those found are placed in cardboard boxes overnight to recover before being released from coastal cliffs the following morning.The wider campaign has also received strong community support. A SPEA survey involving 207 island residents recorded unanimous backing for the blackout initiative.A conservation effort making a differenceThe impact extends well beyond Corvo. According to The Guardian, more than 30,000 Cory's shearwater fledglings have been rescued across the Azores since 2015, including approximately 6,000 on Corvo alone.Research conducted through the international EELabs project has also highlighted the relationship between artificial lighting and seabird disorientation. Preliminary monitoring on Corvo found that approximately 85% of incidents involving grounded young shearwaters occurred when streetlights were switched on.SPEA's work through international conservation projects, including EELabs and LuMinAves, aims to encourage other communities to adopt measures that reduce light pollution.Letting nature find its wayCorvo's initiative also offers a practical lesson for destinations beyond Portugal. Conservation does not always require expensive infrastructure or sweeping interventions. Shielding streetlights, reducing illumination and temporarily switching off unnecessary lighting can all help protect vulnerable wildlife.For an island of just 450 people, the effort has created an example with international relevance. By allowing darkness to reclaim its streets for a few hours each night, Corvo is helping young seabirds find their way home to the ocean.Images Courtesy: istock

articles.title: NASA Administrator defends Learjet copilot after Florida crash
articles.summary: Jared Isaacman took to social media to defend the 20-year-old copilot of the Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida on Nov. 1, killing all nine aboard.
articles.body:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman took to his personal social media account Nov. 2 to defend the female co-pilot of the Learjet that crashed near Palm Beach, Florida.

The private jet, bound from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, plummeted into the ground Nov. 1 near Greenacres and exploded into a fireball. All nine people onboard were killed.

The cause of the crash was not immediately known, but heavy rainfall and thunderstorms were occurring in the area at the time the jet went down, forecaster AccuWeather said in a statement.

Moments before the crash, a person in the cockpit said the crew was "managing the ice," encountering "moderate" turbulence and seeking "better rides," according to audio posted by LiveATC, a website that broadcasts air traffic control communications. That dramatic audio led to significant online criticism of the 20-year-old co-pilot, Nathalia Filgueiras, from Boca Raton. The pilot has not been identified.

"Let people investigate, learn, and share the facts," Isaacman wrote on X. "Be respectful to those who perished and the families who carry their memories. God bless them and their loved ones."

NASA Administrator defends Learjet copilot

"Writing this in my personal capacity, but I have been flying these types of aircraft for more than 20 years, with over 8,000 hours, and have reasonable familiarity with how the charter world operates. I feel compelled to post after seeing commentary about the Lear 60 crash, from missile strikes to DEI to critiquing this poor woman's final radio calls," Isaacman wrote.

Isaacman is an experienced jet pilot and commercial astronaut. He bankrolled and organized two orbital spaceflights with SpaceX. Both included women onboard, and his first, Inspiration4, featured a female pilot , Sian Proctor.

The NASA administrator went on to state that Filgueiras remained professional throughout the situation, knowing her life was about to end. She communicated with air traffic control right up until the crash.

"She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die," he wrote.

"I understand the public interest given the footage and audio. But you do not know the aircraft's maintenance history, whether there was a structural failure, if any failure was induced by turbulence, overspeed, or overcontrol, or everything happening in that cockpit," Isaacman wrote.

The leaked cockpit communication with air traffic control revealed that the crew saw ice and experienced turbulence before the crash occurred.

Isaacman said that it is common for charter companies, which fly these small jets, to hire fairly new commercial pilots and enable them to gain experience before many become commercial pilots. Filgueiras would have likely had all the applicable training, requirements, and checkouts required from the Federal Aviation Administration, he wrote.

Evidence suggests the aircraft began breaking apart before impact, National Transportation Safety Board member Thomas Chapman said at a Monday news conference.

Brooke Edwards is a Space Reporter for Florida Today. Contact her at bedwards@floridatoday.com or on X: @brookeofstars .

articles.title: 2 Words in an Overlooked Flight Log Reveal a Chilling Detail About The Hiroshima Bombing
articles.summary: Still learning, 80 years later.
articles.body:
At 8.15 in the morning of 6 August 1945, the gates to hell opened on the Japanese city of Hiroshima when the US military unleashed the nuclear bomb.

As tens of thousands of people died on the ground below, the American bomber Enola Gay that dropped the warhead soared away. Meanwhile, a growing cloud of soot and smoke began to billow up from the firestorm that raged in the wake of the devastating detonation.

Just 97 minutes later, at 10.52 am Tinian time, navigator Theodore Van Kirk made a brief entry in the aircraft's flight log in scrawled uppercase letters.

That tiny, overlooked detail has now given scientists a new window into the world's only nuclear firestorm on record.

According to a paper led by atmospheric scientist David Romps of the University of California, Berkeley, that note suggests that the plume of soot had risen at least 11.3 kilometers (7 miles) into the sky.

"The Hiroshima firestorm lofted soot well into the upper troposphere, consistent with nuclear-winter scenarios," the team writes in a paper published in Geophysical Research Letters .

The aftermath of a nuclear bomb is chaos. The explosion itself and its mushroom cloud are over relatively quickly, but the intense heat the explosion generates can create a furious storm of fires that rampages for hours.

As the fires lit by the explosion of the Little Boy atomic bomb spread and merged across Hiroshima, the blazing temperatures generated powerful updrafts that carried smoke and soot high into the atmosphere, forming a towering column of cloud.

Just how high that cloud can rise is crucial to understanding the consequences of nuclear warfare.

If enough soot reaches the stratosphere, it can linger for months or years, blocking sunlight and cooling the planet below.

In a large-scale nuclear conflict, the cumulative effects of many such fires could trigger a nuclear winter, with potentially catastrophic consequences for agriculture and food supplies around the world.

But some scientists have disagreed about whether nuclear firestorms can carry soot high enough. Some simulations suggest that most soot would remain in the lower atmosphere, where rain could wash it out before it had a lasting effect on the global climate.

The problem here – and thankfully so – is that we have very few real-world observations of nuclear firestorms. In fact, the bombing of Hiroshima is the only known instance; none eventuated from the bombing of Nagasaki three days later.

Previous researchers have tried to reconstruct the height of the Hiroshima plume using historical photographs, but the results relied on several uncertainties.

Romps and his colleagues, however, found another source of evidence in the historical record.

And their calculation is stunningly clever.

The movements of Enola Gay that day are documented in detail, almost down to the minute. When Van Kirk noted "CLOUD GONE" at 97 minutes after the detonation, the plane was an estimated 750 to 764 kilometers away, at an altitude of around 7,440 meters (24,400 feet).

And that suggests that the cloud was not quite so gone as the log indicates, but that, from their position, the crew could no longer see it.

A separate military memorandum recorded that the crew's "observation was then limited by haze and not curvature of the Earth."

That means that the cloud had not dipped below the horizon. It was obscured instead by atmospheric haze.

This distinction is key – because if the cloud was still above the horizon from such a vast distance, then it must have been extraordinarily tall.

So, by calculating how far the crew could have seen from their altitude, the researchers could work backward to determine the minimum height of the plume.

But this isn't necessarily straightforward, either.

Light doesn't travel through Earth's atmosphere in perfectly straight lines. As air density changes with altitude, light bends slightly toward the surface, allowing us to see a little farther around Earth's curvature than geometry alone would suggest.

Accounting for this required the researchers to reconstruct the atmospheric conditions on the day of the bombing.

Using three historical weather reconstructions, they estimated how temperature and air pressure changed with altitude, allowing them to calculate how light would have bent through the atmosphere that day.

They then ran 100,000 simulations to account for uncertainties in the aircraft's position, altitude, and the atmospheric conditions.

This, obviously, still leaves a not insignificant degree of uncertainty.

But even so, the researchers calculated with 95 percent confidence that the plume must have reached a minimum height of 11.3 kilometers – consistent with nuclear winter scenarios.

Now, the Hiroshima bombing did not cause nuclear winter. But nuclear winter is not expected to result from a single explosion. Rather, it is the potential cumulative consequence of vast amounts of soot injected into the atmosphere by multiple nuclear firestorms ignited during a nuclear war.

What Hiroshima shows is that nuclear firestorms can loft soot to altitudes relevant to this concept – an important piece of evidence consistent with the possibility of nuclear winter.

Let us truly hope the world never has to find out the hard way.

The research has been published in Geophysical Research Letters .

articles.title: Meet Ramya Manjunath Anche, the Bengaluru-born astronomer leading NASA's $20 million PUFFINS telescope mission to study tiny dust particles between stars
articles.summary: This is the story of Ramya Manjunath Anche, a Bengaluru-born astronomer preparing to study something that has remained difficult for scientists to
articles.body: This is the story of Ramya Manjunath Anche, a Bengaluru-born astronomer preparing to study something that has remained difficult for scientists to understand for decades. The subject is of the tiny particles of dust floating between stars. As a teenager fascinated by the 2003 Space Shuttle Columbia disaster, she has now grown up to lead a NASA-funded space telescope mission worth $20 million.Anche is now working as an assistant research professor at the University of Arizona’s Steward Observatory as the principal investigator of NASA’s PUFFINS mission. The aim of the mission is to investigate interstellar dust using a specialised ultraviolet telescope. The mission, selected under NASA’s Astrophysics Pioneers programme, received $20 million in funding in October 2026 and is targeted for launch in 2030.What makes her achievement interesting is that the scientist leading this ambitious international project began her journey in Devanahalli, a town near Bengaluru, India. She then went on to pursue engineering and astrophysics in India before taking her research career to the United States.Journey from a curious schoolgirl to an astronomerRamya Anche comes from a family where science was a regular subject of conversation. Her father, A Manjunath, is a microbiologist retired from the University of Agricultural Sciences in Bengaluru. His work in soil research at home helped nurture her curiosity from an early age.She attended Oxford English School in Devanahalli before studying at MES Vidyasagar Prof. MPL Sastry PU College in Bengaluru. She subsequently pursued a Bachelor of Engineering degree in electrical and electronics engineering from Sir M Visvesvaraya Institute of Technology.In an interview with The Indian Express, Anche said that she was always interested in research and that her family never pressured her to take up a conventional job.Space Shuttle Columbia disasterIt was the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster on February 1, 2003 that influenced her decision. The accident claimed the lives of seven astronauts and left a deep impression on her as a teenager and prompted her to wonder why the tragedy had happened. She went so deep that she wanted to understand whether it could have been prevented.The journey from electrical engineering to astrophysicsIn 2012, Anche joined the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru for an integrated MTech-PhD programme in astronomical instrumentation. Her academic journey subsequently took her to Pune, where she completed a postdoctoral fellowship at the Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (IUCAA) during 2020–21.In 2021, she moved to the United States. She was admitted to the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory and her work focuses on astronomical polarimetry, optical design, high-contrast imaging and the development of space telescopes.But one of the biggest milestones in her career came when she led a proposal for a NASA mission while still working as a postdoctoral researcher. The proposal eventually secured funding under NASA's Astrophysics Pioneers programme.What exactly is PUFFINS, the $20-million mission study?PUFFINS stands for Polarimetry in the Ultraviolet to Find Features in INterStellar Dust.These particles, known as interstellar dust grains, are incredibly small. As per the University of Arizona, PUFFINS will investigate grains smaller than approximately 50 nanometres, roughly the size of a common cold virus.Interstellar dust influences how light travels through space and is also connected to the formation of new stars and planets. Studying its composition, formation and behaviour can therefore help scientists understand how galaxies evolve and how the building blocks of planetary systems come together.To achieve this, PUFFINS will carry a specialised telescope measuring just 10 inches across, approximately the size of a large dinner plate. The mission will use a technique called ultraviolet spectropolarimetry.A team of 40 researchers and a 2030 launch targetAlthough Anche is leading the mission, PUFFINS is a collaboration of scientific efforts involving the University of Arizona, McDonald Observatory at the University of Texas at Austin and researchers from several institutions around the world.Around 40 scientists, engineers, graduate students and postdoctoral researchers are involved in the project. The team is currently in the early design phase, with the next four years expected to involve designing and building the telescope before its planned launch in 2030.

articles.title: A truck-sized NASA space telescope is about to crash to Earth
articles.summary: NASA’s Swift Observatory is now about to fall back to Earth on Wednesday after attempts to push it back into a higher orbit failed.﻿
articles.body: Almost 22 years after it was launched, NASA’s Swift Observatory is now about to fall back to Earth on Wednesday after attempts to push it back into a higher orbit failed. NASA announced that the aging space telescope is anticipated to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere at approximately 3:30AM ET (give or take 11 hours), and that it expects most of the spacecraft to burn up, but some components will likely survive re-entry. The observatory weighs around 3,200 pounds and measures in at 5.6 meters (18.4 feet) high and 5.4 meters (17.7 feet) wide, though much of the latter includes its deployable solar arrays. The risk of surviving components causing any harm is low, according to NASA: > “Re-entry locations of any surviving components can vary from hemisphere to hemisphere and depend on when it re-enters. Due to Swift’s low inclination, re-entry locations of surviving fragments are limited between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude. The risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely — approximately 1 in 2,100. NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions.” The agency gave up on trying to save the falling telescope earlier this year, after the Link spacecraft that was attempting the rescue experienced technical issues with attitude control. Still, Swift far outlived its original two-year prime mission to study the origin of gamma-ray bursts, and went on to serve as a general-purpose multi-wavelength observatory until solar storms pushed it into a lower orbit. You can follow Swift’s descent by monitoring NASA’s blog for continued updates.

articles.title: In 2024, researchers began hanging different coloured and patterned sheets inside a Canadian seabird colony; by 2026, their study found stripes caused 2.8 times fewer bird collisions than plain sheets
articles.summary: Researchers in Canada have found that changing the colour or pattern of a surface could help prevent seabirds from crashing into illuminated structures at
articles.body: Researchers in Canada have found that changing the colour or pattern of a surface could help prevent seabirds from crashing into illuminated structures at night. In experiments conducted during 2024 and 2025 on Bon Portage Island in Nova Scotia, scientists found that Leach’s Storm-Petrels were less likely to collide with dark or patterned sheets than with plain white ones. Vertically striped sheets recorded 2.8 times fewer bird collisions than plain sheets. The findings were published in the journal Ornithological Applications, Oxford University Press reported.The study examined a problem affecting seabirds that travel or search for food at night. Artificial lights from coastal buildings, fishing vessels and offshore industrial facilities can disturb their movements. Some birds become stranded near these lights, while others collide with structures. Such incidents can cause injuries or leave birds exposed to exhaustion, dehydration and predators.Turning off lights can reduce these risks, but it is not always possible. Ports, industrial sites and other workplaces often need lighting to protect workers. Researchers therefore wanted to know whether changing the appearance of walls and other upright surfaces could make them safer for birds without requiring the lights to be switched off.The team, comprising Alina Rutherford, Michael Robertson, Linda Hutchinson and Dave Shutler, tested this idea in a breeding colony of Leach’s Storm-Petrels. The species, scientifically known as Hydrobates leucorhous, is classified as vulnerable globally. Bon Portage Island is home to around 39,000 breeding pairs, making it the largest colony of the species in Nova Scotia.How researchers tested colours and patternsThe experiments took place over 40 nights across two years. In 2024, researchers tested different colours over 28 nights between July and September. The following year, they examined patterns over another 12 nights between June and August.They suspended cloth sheets measuring approximately 2.3 metres by 2.6 metres from poles inside the colony. The sheets acted as substitutes for walls or other vertical surfaces that birds might encounter near artificial lighting.During the first year, the team used white, beige and black sheets. These colours were selected to compare how much light each surface reflected and to represent colours commonly found on buildings.In 2025, the researchers used plain white sheets alongside sheets marked with vertical stripes or grid patterns. Black fabric paint covered approximately half of each patterned sheet.Floodlights illuminated the sheets, switching on and off at five-minute intervals. Researchers changed the sheet being tested every 30 minutes and recorded how many birds collided with it.The experiment was designed to avoid harming the birds. If a bird repeatedly struck a sheet, researchers temporarily switched off the light. Birds that remained in the area were moved to a dark location.What the experiments revealedThe results showed a strong connection between artificial lighting and collisions. Storm-petrels were approximately nine times more likely to strike the sheets when the lights were switched on than when they were off.Colour also made a difference. White sheets recorded 2.7 times more individual bird collisions than black sheets. The white material reflected almost five times as much light as the black material.Patterns produced another important result. Compared with plain sheets, those marked with grids recorded 2.4 times fewer individual bird collisions, while vertically striped sheets recorded 2.8 times fewer.When researchers counted every collision, including repeated strikes by the same bird, the differences were even greater. Grid-patterned sheets recorded 3.4 times fewer total collisions, while striped sheets recorded 3.7 times fewer.The findings suggest that darker surfaces and visible patterns could make illuminated structures less dangerous for seabirds.Why artificial light may confuse seabirdsResearchers also observed something unexpected. Although more birds collided with sheets when the lights were on, fewer birds appeared to be flying overhead during illuminated periods.When the lights were switched on, birds flying above the experimental area often scattered. This suggested that artificial light might not simply attract birds at close range.Instead, the researchers said the light could be interfering with their ability to recognise and avoid nearby objects.The exact reason remains uncertain. Artificial lighting may interfere with visual or navigational signals, or its brightness may temporarily affect the birds' vision.Could changing wall colours save seabirds?The researchers believe darker or patterned walls could offer a practical way to reduce collisions at coastal facilities, ships and offshore platforms.Patterns may be particularly useful where lighting must remain bright for worker safety. In the experiment, patterned sheets reduced collisions even when the overall amount of reflected light was approximately equal to that of plain sheets.However, the team cautioned that the method has so far been tested inside a breeding colony, not at industrial locations where seabirds become stranded.Further research is needed to establish whether changing real building surfaces would produce similar results and whether the approach could protect birds without compromising human safety.

articles.title: A Florida schoolgirl who saw her local waterways deteriorating began collecting discarded oyster shells; her project has amassed 1,600 pounds of shells and drawn more than 60 students and teachers
articles.summary: Some children are born observant and intelligent. They are active with the happenings around them and always look for solution.
articles.body: Some children are born observant and intelligent. They are active with the happenings around them and always look for solution. Meet Bianca Bernhard, whose concern about deteriorating water quality led her to create the Martin Oyster Restoration Initiative, or MORI, an initiative for the waterways in the area that motivated the entire school to practice conservation. According to online media reports. at South Fork High School in Florida, discarded oyster shells are being given a second life, with students helping turn restaurant waste into material that can support oyster restoration and healthier waterways.Turning restaurant waste into restorationRather than treating used oyster shells as rubbish, MORI collects them from restaurants and prepares them for future restoration projects. According to WFLX, the idea took shape after Bernhard became concerned about the condition of local waterways while rowing.As per the report, the shells are brought back to South Fork High School, where they go through a preparation process before being returned to the environment. They are transported, dried and cured so they can eventually be incorporated into approved reef structures. These structures can provide a foundation for oysters to establish and grow. Oyster populations grow and filter water and provide habitat in aquatic ecosystems, WFLX report explains.For Bernhard, the project has turned an environmental concern into something students can actively participate in rather than simply observe.More than 60 students join the effortMORI has steadily expanded within South Fork High School, bringing together students and teachers from several programmes. Marine science students contribute to the environmental side of the project, while construction and agriculture students can support other stages of the work.According to WPTV, the initiative has now involved more than 60 students and teachers and collected approximately 1,600 pounds of oyster shells.The programme also connects conservation with education. Participating students can earn honour credits through the school's Marine Sciences programme, giving them an opportunity to combine academic learning with practical environmental work. The result is a project that goes beyond shell collection. Students get to see how material that would otherwise be discarded can become part of a restoration effort.From school grounds to the Indian River LagoonMORI's reach has also extended beyond the campus. The initiative is working with Docks for a Clean Lagoon, a nonprofit involved in creating vertical oyster gardens.According to WFLX, shells prepared and cured by South Fork volunteers have been used in the development of vertical oyster gardens intended for the Indian River Lagoon.These structures are designed to provide additional surfaces for oysters to grow, supporting restoration work while giving students a tangible connection to projects taking place in local waterways.Recognition beyond FloridaBernhard's conservation work has also brought wider attention. WPTV reports that she is a finalist in the Blue Hatchling Youth category of Loggerhead Marinelife Center's 2026 Go Blue Awards. The awards recognise young people, nonprofits, businesses and individuals involved in ocean conservation and efforts to protect marine ecosystems.Bernhard's recognition comes as MORI looks towards expansion. Her plans include bringing the programme to three additional local schools during the 2026-27 school year.A student project with bigger ambitionsThe next phase could also involve research. According to WFLX, Bernhard hopes to work with the Florida Oceanographic Society on oyster restoration research and involve students in developing additional restoration structures.A concern first noticed from a rowing boat has therefore evolved into a growing school-led initiative. With thousands of pounds of shells diverted from waste streams and dozens of students taking part, MORI is showing how environmental restoration can begin with a simple idea and grow through community involvement.Images Courtesy: MORI

articles.title: Giannis Antetokounmpo’s family foundation teamed up with a marine-cleanup group in 2026, transforming discarded fishing gear into basketball nets for public courts across Athens and replacing 80 worn nets
articles.summary: A collaboration between basketball and marine conservation has given discarded fishing equipment a second life on public courts in Athens.
articles.body: A collaboration between basketball and marine conservation has given discarded fishing equipment a second life on public courts in Athens. The Charles Antetokounmpo Family Foundation (CAFF), established by NBA star Giannis Antetokounmpo and his family, partnered with Greek marine-cleanup organisation Enaleia to replace worn-out basketball nets with new ones made from recycled fishing gear. According to reports by Enaleia, B2Green and Dnews in April and May 2026, the initiative was carried out in cooperation with OPANDA, the cultural, sports and youth organisation of the Municipality of Athens. The project focuses on a problem that often goes unnoticed in discussions about marine pollution: discarded fishing equipment. Nets and other fishing materials can remain in the marine environment long after they have stopped serving their original purpose, posing a threat to marine ecosystems and wildlife.The replacement work covered 80 basketball nets that were either damaged or had been removed from outdoor courts. The new nets were produced in Greece using discarded fishing equipment collected through designated port reception facilities. Rather than allowing the material to become another source of marine waste, the partners found a way to repurpose it for everyday public use.The installations have been spread across neighbourhoods throughout Athens, including Sepolia, Pangrati, Exarchia, Neos Kosmos and Kypseli. The project also extends to courts in areas such as Koukaki, Metaxourgeio and Ampelokipoi, bringing the recycled equipment into spaces used by local residents and young basketball players.The environmental organisation behind the initiative, Enaleia, works with a network of more than 6,000 fishers to recover marine plastic and used fishing equipment. Its work includes collecting discarded materials before they re-enter the marine environment and finding ways to put them back into productive use through recycling and upcycling.For the Antetokounmpo family, the partnership also builds on a longstanding connection between basketball and community development. Through CAFF, the family supports programmes centred on sport, education and opportunities for young people. Its AntetokounBros Academy, for instance, has provided basketball training and life-skills opportunities to children from financially vulnerable backgrounds in Athens.What makes the initiative interesting is that it takes an environmental problem and turns it into something people can actually see and use. Discarded fishing nets are often out of sight once they are pulled from the water, but their impact on marine life can last much longer. By giving these materials a new purpose on basketball courts, the project brings the idea of recycling into everyday spaces. For children and young players using these courts, the new nets are also a small reminder that even waste can be put to better use.The project also gives young players and local residents a chance to realise how small changes can make a difference. Basketball courts are used by people of all ages, making them a natural place to bring this message closer to the community. Instead of letting old fishing nets go to waste, the partnership has found a way to turn them into something useful again. By bringing recycled fishing gear onto neighbourhood basketball courts, the collaboration connects two causes that are particularly relevant to the city: access to public sporting facilities and the protection of marine ecosystems. It also offers a practical example of how materials typically associated with ocean pollution can be repurposed for something communities use every day.

articles.title: Orbital Matter 3D-printed the first rigid beam in the vacuum of space | TechCrunch
articles.summary: An in-space construction first could be an enabler for the space data centers of the future.
articles.body:
A satellite built by the German startup Orbital Matter 3D-printed a half-meter long beam out of a custom plastic material, in what executives called a first for a free-flying spacecraft in orbit, and a step toward constructing large structures in space.

The company’s small satellite, Replicator 2, was launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission this summer, with four of the company’s 3D printers onboard. Each printer can create a rigid, cylindrical beam by extruding coils of resin that are cured by an ultraviolet light, which the company analogizes to cement and water.

This technology matters because future spacecraft will need to be larger in order to generate more electrical power and radiate a more heat into the vacuum of space, particularly if they’re going to serve as orbital data centers. But they’ll still need to fit into the tight confines of the fairing on top of the rocket that carries them into orbit. If spacecraft are able to construct their own structures in orbit, the power and heat-dissipation challenges may get a lot easier to solve.

“Replicator 2 is the first proof that we can simply build the array in space, at whatever size the mission demands,” said Jakub Stojek, CEO and co-founder of Orbital Matter. The company is partnering with the European Space Agency and Thales Alenia, a leading European satellite builder, with which it collaborated on Replicator 2.

Today’s large structures in space are origami projects — large solar arrays or telescope mirrors are folded up and then deployed on orbit. That’s a tricky engineering project, and so the idea of making and assembling those structures in space is appealing. NASA has funded some efforts at the idea, notably a mission with the company Redwire that 3D-printed structural beams in a vacuum chamber in 2023 but never got off the ground.

Two of Orbital Matter’s printers are designed to deploy a flexible solar array, but an anomaly led one of the printers to fail. Still, the boom that was created successfully deployed the solar array, and is an important proof of concept. Previous 3D-printing efforts in microgravity were limited to the pressurized environment onboard the International Space Station.

“That’s why we put so many printers on this single satellite. We preferred to learn in orbit and adapt the software as needed rather than waste years testing every possibility on the ground,” Orbital Matters CTO Robert Ihnatisin told TechCrunch.

The boom’s length is limited by the amount of resin carried onboard the satellite, and the company’s engineers believe that 100 meter booms are feasible. For comparison, SpaceX’s Starlink V2 satellites — among the most powerful mass-produced satellites in orbit — uses solar arrays that are 20 meters long.

Orbital Matter was co-founded in 2022 by Ihnatsin, who previously worked at 3D-printing company FormLabs, and Stojek, and raised a $3 million seed round.

Now, Orbital Matter is working on another demonstration mission, scheduled for launch in 2028, that will test a larger version of its printer on a bigger satellite that the company hopes will deploy a solar array that can generate 5 kw of power. That will be a “stepping stone” toward larger deployments of 100+ KW per wing by 2030.

The company is also collaborating with satellite builders that are considering incorporating its PADS (printer-assisted deployment system) into their spacecraft to extend solar panels, antennas, or other components.

articles.title: A 113-million-year-old baby dinosaur found in South Korea has been named after cartoon character Dooly, revealing the country’s first dinosaur skull remains
articles.summary: A rare dinosaur fossil found in South Korea has been identified as a new species, the country’s first new dinosaur species in 15 years.
articles.body: A rare dinosaur fossil found in South Korea has been identified as a new species, the country’s first new dinosaur species in 15 years. The skeleton was found on the Aphae Islands off the country’s southwestern coast and dates to around 113 million years ago. Researchers named it Doolysaurus huhmin after Dooly, a South Korean cartoon character.The remains include parts of the skull, the first dinosaur skull material found in the country. According to the Natural History Museum, the animal was likely still a juvenile when it died and measured a couple of feet in length. The discovery is significant because dinosaur bones are rare in South Korea, despite the region’s record of footprints and eggshells.Dooly-named baby dinosaur fossil reveals South Korea’s first skull remainsResearchers found the fossil during an excavation at a site on the Aphae Islands, off South Korea’s southwestern coast. It was preserved inside solid rock. Researchers noticed gastroliths, or stomach stones, beside leg bones emerging from the rock and suspected that more of the animal might be preserved.They used a micro-CT scanner to examine the specimen. The scan revealed parts of the ribs and arm bones, as well as elements of the head. These skull pieces are the first dinosaur skull remains found in South Korea. The discovery matters because dinosaur body fossils are much rarer in the country than footprints and eggshells. The find provides rare physical evidence of a dinosaur that lived in the region.Baby dinosaur fossil reveals its age, size and possible feather coveringThe fossil dates to around 113 million years ago. Researchers estimate that the dinosaur was about two years old when it died. Growth markers in its bones indicate that it was still growing, and the team estimates that an adult may have been about twice its size. The youngster measured just a couple of feet in length.Researchers suspect it may have had a fuzzy covering of feathers. The gastroliths found beside its bones suggest that it was omnivorous and ate a varied diet. The animal was a thescelosaurid, a type of small two-legged dinosaur. These were early relatives of larger plant-eaters such as Iguanodon.New dinosaur species named after South Korean cartoon character DoolyThe researchers chose the name Doolysaurus huhmin because the young dinosaur resembles Dooly, a familiar character from South Korean children’s television. Created by Kim Soo-jung, Dooly the Little Dinosaur is a baby dinosaur with tufts sprouting from its head. Jongyun Jung, who led the research describing the new species, said, “Dooly is one of the very famous, iconic dinosaur characters in Korea.”“Every generation in Korea knows this character. And our specimen is also a juvenile or ‘baby’, so it’s perfect for our dinosaur species name to honour Dooly.”The species was described by researchers from the University of Texas at Austin and the Korean Dinosaur Research Center.Why dinosaur bones are rare despite South Korea’s rich footprint recordDoolysaurus huhmin is only the third named dinosaur species discovered in South Korea. The country has a rich record of dinosaur footprints, studied extensively, but fossilised bones are much harder to find. The region where the footprints formed was probably a tidal mudflat. Tracks left by dinosaurs crossing the soft ground were readily preserved, while skeletal remains were less likely to survive.Researchers have found evidence of many kinds of dinosaurs in the area, including small and large plant-eaters and meat-eating species. The new skeleton adds to the limited record of dinosaur body fossils from Korea.

articles.title: Medieval Humans Partly Caused Two Catastrophic Lake Tsunamis, And We Could Easily Do It Again, Scientists Warn
articles.summary: Can we learn from their mistakes?
articles.body:
Tsunamis are not exclusive to the ocean: with the right conditions, they can happen in lakes, too.

At Lake Iseo in northern Italy, medieval humans set the scene for two such catastrophic wave events, and researchers are warning that it could easily happen again.

In a paper published in Nature Communications , an international team has brought together data from sediment cores, seismic profiles, a medieval manuscript, archaeological records, and the modern-day lake itself.

This range of sources helped them recreate the unusual medieval disasters via computer models.

Lake Iseo is downstream of the Italian Alps, from which it receives a regular supply of water via snowmelt. The same tectonic activity that helped to form the Alps also brings the occasional earthquake to the region.

Two thousand years of intensifying land use changed the way sediment settled in the delta, making its sides steeper.

Before the Middle Ages, the Oglio River delta was surrounded by forest. When it rained, loose sediment would flow downhill, but its passage was slowed by the dense networks of tree roots and fungi that held the soil together.

Underwater, the delta's slopes were gentle, gradually tilting towards the lake's deepest point, which is around 250 meters.

But things rapidly changed around the fall of the Roman Empire.

In the centuries that followed, more and more forests that once surrounded the delta were removed for pasture and mining; the human population grew; and three times more sediment was flushed into the lake each year on average.

More and more sediment accumulated at the lake's northern end, creating precariously steep underwater banks just waiting to crash.

And that's exactly what happened, twice.

The natural shape of the delta could handle some seismic activity from time to time without necessarily flooding the surrounding towns.

But when the violent 1117 CE Verona Earthquake shook the lake's steepened banks, they collapsed in an underwater landslide, displacing a massive amount of water that, according to the researchers' modeling, would have flooded large sections of the shores of Lake Iseo without a minute's warning.

"Our simulations reveal that the medieval delta collapses in Lake Iseo generated some of the largest subaquatic landslide-induced tsunamis ever inferred in a lacustrine setting," the study's authors write .

By their calculations, waves in the northern part of the lake would have exceeded 50 meters, inundating nearby shores in less than a minute, with water reaching up to 2.7 kilometers inland.

A 12th-century manuscript now held at the Vatican Library describes the catastrophic event in vivid detail that matches the modeling well. The passage is translated to English as follows:

"The lake overflowed so much that very few of the inhabitants of the nearby villages escaped this danger. Many castles and fortresses also collapsed miserably, with the destruction of their inhabitants."

But alas, medieval folks are not especially known for their scientific inquiry – disasters like this were more likely seen as a message from God. They rebuilt, and resumed the practices that had led to the first fatal tsunami.

Just over a century later, a second earthquake hit: the 1222 CE Brescia earthquake .

Another large tsunami ensued in Lake Iseo, with waves peaking at around 13 meters, and water rushing up to 1 kilometer inland.

"Both tsunamis propagated rapidly across Lake Iseo and were strongly influenced by Monte Isola, the central island, which acts as a natural barrier, splitting the waves and partially shielding the cities behind it," the authors explain .

"Despite this protection, areas such as [the town of] Iseo still experienced significant impacts, with maximum wave heights of ~5.5 meters (1117 CE) and ~2 meters (1222 CE), arriving ~7 minutes after the landslides."

Lake Iseo now has the most densely built shores of any lake in the Italian Alps. Meanwhile, more than eight centuries' worth of sediment has built up since the 1222 CE collapse.

"A tsunami comparable in magnitude to the catastrophic events that struck Lake Iseo during the medieval period would cause severe devastation today, given the region's dense population and shoreline development," the authors write .

"A global lake synthesis showed that human-driven erosion has reached its highest levels since the Industrial Era, progressively overloading deltas worldwide; thus, similar catastrophic failures may become more likely in the future."

The research has been published in Nature Communications .

articles.title: Nasa drilled a Martian rock in 2020 and stored the findings for years; scientists have now identified seven organic molecules never detected on Mars before
articles.summary: Organic molecules on Mars have reached a new record of diversity, with seven never detected on the planet before.
articles.body: Organic molecules on Mars have reached a new record of diversity, with seven never detected on the planet before. The Curiosity rover drilled the rock sample, nicknamed Mary Anning 3, in October 2020, and years of laboratory analysis have identified 21 carbon-containing molecules inside it, the most varied collection ever found on the Red Planet. Scientists have no way of knowing whether biological or geological processes made them, and either explanation remains possible. What the results do show is that ancient Mars had the chemistry to support life, and that such molecules can survive for billions of years despite radiation.Why a clay-rich rock on Mount Sharp was the ideal place to preserve ancient organic compoundsAccording toNasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, the sample came from a part of Mount Sharp that lakes and streams covered billions of years ago. That oasis surged and dried up several times, eventually enriching the area with clay minerals, which are especially good at preserving organic compounds. These are carbon-containing molecules that act as building blocks of life and occur throughout the solar system. The sample’s nickname honours Mary Anning, an English fossil collector and palaeontologist.What the new nitrogen ring and sulphur-bearing molecule could mean for the chemistry behind lifeOne of the new discoveries is a nitrogen heterocycle, a ring of carbon atoms that contains nitrogen. Scientists consider this kind of structure a predecessor to ribonucleic acid and deoxyribonucleic acid, the nucleic acids that carry genetic information. Amy Williams of the University of Florida, lead author of the paper published in Nature Communications, said the detection is “pretty profound” because such structures can be chemical precursors to more complex nitrogen-bearing molecules. She added that nitrogen heterocycles had never been found on the Martian surface or confirmed in Martian meteorites.The other standout is benzothiophene, which contains carbon and sulphur and has turned up in many meteorites. Some scientists think those meteorites, and the organic molecules inside them, seeded prebiotic chemistry across the early solar system.How a laboratory inside the rover’s belly turns drilled Martian rock into a list of moleculesCuriosity carries a miniature laboratory called Sample Analysis at Mars in its belly. A drill on the rover’s robotic arm pulverises a carefully chosen rock into powder and trickles it into the laboratory. There, a high-temperature oven releases gases, and instruments analyse them to reveal the rock’s composition. The laboratory can also perform wet chemistry, dropping samples into a small cup of solvent whose reactions break apart larger molecules that would otherwise be hard to detect.Only two cups hold tetramethylammonium hydroxide, a powerful solution reserved for the highest-value samples, and Mary Anning 3 was the first to be exposed to it. Curiosity has since used the second and final cup at weblike boxwork ridges formed by ancient groundwater, and the team will analyse those results for a future peer-reviewed paper.The same laboratory made last year’s discovery of the largest organic molecules found on Mars, long-chain hydrocarbons including decane, undecane and dodecane. Ashwin Vasavada, the mission’s project scientist at Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said it took dozens of scientists and engineers to locate the site, drill the sample and make these discoveries.How a meteorite older than four billion years showed where the Martian molecules could come fromTo check how the solvent reacts with material from beyond Earth, the paper’s authors tested the technique on a piece of the Murchison meteorite, one of the most studied meteorites of all time. It is more than four billion years old and contains organic molecules seeded throughout the early solar system. Once exposed to the solvent, the sample broke much larger molecules into some of those seen in Mary Anning 3, including benzothiophene. That shows the Martian molecules could have formed from the breakdown of even more complex compounds relevant to life.How the discovery prepares the next instruments bound for Mars and Saturn’s moon TitanSample Analysis at Mars was built by Nasa’s Goddard Space Flight Centre in Greenbelt, Maryland, and is based on larger commercial-grade laboratory instruments. Engineers had to shrink it dramatically and make it run on less power. Scientists also learned to heat its oven more slowly, over longer periods, to carry out some of the experiments.Charles Malespin, the instrument’s principal investigator at Nasa Goddard and a coauthor of the study, said that working out how to do this chemistry on Mars for the first time was a feat. He added that the team is now prepared to run similar experiments on future missions.Nasa Goddard has supplied several components, including the mass spectrometer, for the Mars Organic Molecular Analyser, a next-generation version heading to the European Space Agency’s Rosalind Franklin Mars rover. A similar instrument, the Dragonfly Mass Spectrometer, will explore Saturn’s moon Titan aboard Nasa’s Dragonfly rotorcraft. Both can perform wet chemistry with the same solvent.

articles.title: A butterfly disappeared from Ontario in 1988 and has not been recorded there since; nearly four decades later, scientists plan to bring eggs from New York and breed the species for release into restored Canadian habitat
articles.summary: What if one day you discover the world has no butterflies? Their velvety wings, dashing through the garden, a moving pop of colour in a world of darkness.
articles.body: What if one day you discover the world has no butterflies? Their velvety wings, dashing through the garden, a moving pop of colour in a world of darkness.Butterflies are not just there for aesthetic purposes. Their most important job is pollinating; a reduction in butterfly populations can mean a reduction in plant diversity, since wild plants and flowers will struggle to reproduce. They are also sensitive to environmental shifts. As bioindicators, they can help assess the health of the environment.In Canada, a species of butterfly disappeared from Ontario in 1988 and has not been recorded there since. But now, nearly four decades later, it could flutter back. Scientists are preparing to bring it back, with plans to breed the butterflies in captivity and release them into restored habitats in the province.Which butterfly species has disappeared from Ontario?Meet the frosted elfin (Callophrys irus), a small, rather understated butterfly with delicate wings and a greyish-brown hue. Unlike its more flamboyant cousins, this species is not particularly colourful. Its wingspan measures just 22 to 24 mm, making it easy to miss if you are not looking closely.The butterfly was historically found in southern Ontario, particularly around St. Williams, near the northern shores of Lake Erie. It favours open oak-pine woodlands and nearby clearings where its preferred food plant, wild lupine, grows.The frosted elfin is also a non-migratory species, meaning it does not travel long distances. It depends on its existing habitat, unable to escape unfavourable conditions; thus making the loss of its natural surroundings particularly difficult to overcome.According to the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada, several surveys, including one conducted in 2019, failed to find any trace of the butterfly. Its disappearance is largely attributed to habitat destruction caused by urban development and the conversion of natural landscapes into farmland. As oak savannas and open woodlands gave way to buildings and agricultural fields, the butterfly gradually lost the very environment it needed to survive. While it is still found in parts of the northeastern United States, it has completely disappeared from Ontario.The frosted elfin is not the only butterfly to have made headlines after years of absence. In August 2025, a zebra swallowtail was spotted in Toronto's High Park, attracting considerable attention from butterfly enthusiasts. The striking black-and-white butterfly, recognisable by its long, pointed wings, was last recorded in High Park in 1896. Its most recent recorded appearance in Toronto was in 1952.Scientists' plan to bring back the Frosted ElfinNow a group of Canadian scientists, led by the University of Guelph, is trying to restore the frosted elfin to Ontario. Led by ecologist Ryan Norris, the project will transport adult butterflies and their eggs from New York to the Cambridge Butterfly Conservatory, where they will be bred in captivity and then released into the wild.The first release is planned for spring 2027 in Port Rowan, in Norfolk County, southeast of London, Ontario. However, before the butterflies can make their return, researchers need to ensure that their new home is ready to welcome them, mainly ensuring that there are sufficient wild lupine plants to support the caterpillars once they hatch.The proposed release sites include restored habitats, that were once old tobacco fields but have since developed into thriving oak savanna landscapes. These open woodlands provide the conditions the frosted elfin needs to survive, offering both shelter and access to its host plant.The reintroduction is part of a larger, $2.4-million conservation initiative funded by the federal government through an NSERC Alliance-Society grant. The project aims to recover three at-risk butterfly species across Canada: the frosted elfin, the mottled duskywing and the curiously isolated hairstreak.There is already some encouraging news. The mottled duskywing, a medium-sized butterfly with dark grey and brown wings, was reintroduced at Pinery Provincial Park and other protected areas in Norfolk County around five years ago. Its population has since grown to several hundred at Pinery and close to 100 at another location. Researchers have even spotted the butterflies spreading into nearby campsites and areas outside their regular monitoring sites.The team is also working to strengthen the population of the curiously isolated hairstreak, a rare species found in Waterton Lakes National Park in southern Alberta. With its entire known population concentrated in one location, the butterfly remains vulnerable to natural disasters and other environmental disturbances. Researchers are exploring whether it can be introduced to other suitable habitats.Ultimately, restoring the butterflies means restoring the ecosystems they depend on. Butterflies are one of the most important part of the ecosystem and are essential to a healthy environment. Their disappearance is often a warning that something much larger has gone wrong.

articles.title: In 17th-century Poland, a woman was buried with a sickle across her neck and a stone under her chin to stop her rising from the grave; researchers are now re-examining the so-called ‘vampire’ burial
articles.summary: Vampires are one of the most famous mythological creatures in history. These blood-sucking creatures roam the night searching for people to feed upon.
articles.body: Vampires are one of the most famous mythological creatures in history. These blood-sucking creatures roam the night searching for people to feed upon.Perhaps it is the fascinating legends surrounding these creatures: their sharp fangs, their association with the night, their ability to morph into a bat, or their aversion to garlic (imagine how sad?). Or perhaps it is the actual idea of being a vampire, meaning immortality, that makes them such a fan(g)-favourite.Maybe this fascination and fear led to the unusual burial of a 17th-century Polish woman, found with a padlock on her toe and an iron sickle across her neck. Whether she was a vampire or not, someone went to great lengths to ensure she remained dead.A grave that was anything but ordinaryIn 2022, archaeologists digging through a cemetery in the Polish village of Pień made a rather unsettling discovery. Grave 75 held the remains of a young woman, buried with an iron sickle across her neck, the blade facing her, and a triangular padlock attached to her big toe.The burial dates back to the mid-17th century, and the objects were anything but normal grave offerings. They were put there to keep the dead from coming back into the world of the living. The woman was later named Zosia by archaeologists, in an attempt to restore some of the identity and dignity she had been denied in death.For years, archaeologists led by Dariusz Poliński of Nicolaus Copernicus University studied her remains and the strange objects found with her. The findings, published in 2026 in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports, suggest the local people may have seen Zosia as a threat, associating her with misfortunes such as disease and famine.Interestingly, the burial appeared to have happened in two stages. The padlock was likely attached to her toe during the initial burial. At some point, the grave was reopened, the soil disturbed and the body repositioned before the sickle was placed across her neck. The blade was positioned so that any attempt to rise would potentially result in the woman decapitating herself.What made Zosia so frightening?To understand why someone would go to such lengths to restrain a dead woman, researchers had to look beyond the grave and into the beliefs of 17th-century Poland.At the time of her burial, i.e. 17th century, vampires were not quite the elegant, blood-sucking aristocrats we recognise from modern films. They were considered demonic beings, somewhere between ghosts, witches and the undead. People believed that certain individuals could return after death and bring disease, destruction and misfortune to their communities.One Polish folk belief held that a person could possess two souls. While one remained in the body, the other could wander around causing trouble. A padlock was believed to keep the good soul trapped inside the body and prevent the supposedly evil one from escaping.The fear was not restricted to people who had behaved badly during their lives. Outsiders, religious heretics, orphans and people who died under unusual or tragic circumstances were particularly vulnerable to suspicion. Those who drowned, died by suicide or passed away during childbirth could also be considered potential threats after death.Zosia, however, may have stood out for reasons beyond the circumstances of her death.Examinations of her skeleton revealed that she was approximately 18 years old. She also had a condition known as Kimmerle anomaly, a bony formation on one of her cervical vertebrae. The condition can be associated with headaches, neck pain and fainting spells. Researchers believe these symptoms may have made her appear unusual to people who did not understand her condition.Her bones also showed Harris lines, markers of interruptions in childhood bone growth. They may have been caused by periods of malnutrition, illness or physical stress. More tests revealed a strange growth on her breast bone, possibly a benign tumour or some other abnormality. It could have been a visible lump or a red mark on her chest, depending on its external appearance.A wealthy woman in an unwelcoming graveyardThere is another interesting detail about Zosia's burial. Despite the rather brutal treatment of her remains, evidence suggests that she may have belonged to a wealthy family.Archaeologists discovered delicate silk fibres around her skull, which textile specialists later examined under an electron microscope. The fibres were woven with silver and gold threads, possibly forming an ornamental band on an expensive head-cap.Such cloth was a luxury in 17th century Poland and would have been unavailable to common villagers. The quality of the material suggests that Zosia might have been a member of the upper classes, even perhaps a noblewoman.Her expensive clothing raises another question: why was someone who may have enjoyed considerable wealth buried in such an unusual cemetery?Researchers believe the Pień burial ground may have been unconsecrated land, located away from a church or chapel. It appears to have been used for people who were poor, disgraced or otherwise excluded from conventional burial grounds.Zosia may have belonged to the last category.There is also a possibility that she was not originally from the village. Chemical analysis of her teeth, particularly the strontium isotopes preserved in their enamel, suggested that she could have grown up in several regions across Europe, including southern Sweden or the Upper Rhine region of Germany.Sweden and Poland were involved in military conflict during the 17th century. If Zosia was Swedish, she may have been regarded with considerable hostility by the local population. Her wealth, foreign origins and physical differences could have made her an easy target.An entire cemetery of vampires?As unsettling as Zosia's grave was, it was hardly the only unusual burial discovered in Pień.Archaeologists examined around 100 graves at the cemetery, with more than a dozen displaying what they describe as extraordinary burial practices. These included skeletons weighed down with rocks, a child buried face down with a padlock beneath its foot, and even an infant buried with a lock.A disturbing discovery was a child aged 5-7 with most of the upper body missing. Another burial contained a man and a child in a crucifix position near his feet.The results indicate that the fear of the undead was not aimed at Zosia alone. Even children, who could hardly have posed a threat to anyone during their short lives, were subjected to similar precautions. Such practices were part of a wider wave of vampire hysteria across Eastern and Central Europe.Bringing Zosia back to lifePerhaps the most remarkable part of Zosia's story is that, 350 years after her burial, researchers have managed to give the young woman a face again.Forensic sculptor Oscar Nilsson, who has worked on facial reconstructions for decades, used measurements of her skull, skeletal structure, age and estimated body composition to recreate her appearance. After approximately 150 hours of work, he produced a lifelike reconstruction showing a young woman with blue eyes, light brown hair and a broad nose.The people who buried Zosia did everything they could to prevent her from returning to life. Centuries later, archaeologists and scientists have spent years doing almost the exact opposite.Her story remains incomplete. Researchers still do not know exactly how she died, where she spent her childhood or what happened during her final days. But her burial offers a glimpse into a society where fear could turn a person's differences into something monstrous.After all, vampires may be creatures of folklore, but the fear that creates them is very real. And sometimes, the scariest thing about a vampire story is not the person buried in the grave, but the people who put them there.

articles.title: Meet Zorba, a Belgian Malinois who was India's first dog on anti-poaching duty and helped catch 60 poachers of Assam's rhinos in his eight-year career
articles.summary: In the forests of Assam’s Kaziranga National Park, where one-horned rhinoceroses have long faced the threat of poaching, one of the most determined
articles.body: In the forests of Assam’s Kaziranga National Park, where one-horned rhinoceroses have long faced the threat of poaching, one of the most determined members of the anti-poaching force had four legs, a sharp nose and an extraordinary instinct for following a trail. His name was Zorba, a Belgian Malinois who helped forest officials track down more than 60 poachers during his career. From recovering crucial evidence from a pond to following the blood trail of an injured suspect for nearly 1.5 km, the canine became an unlikely but formidable ally in the fight to protect India’s wildlife.Zorba, who was part of Aaranyak’s K9 unit, India's first dog squad dedicated to wildlife crime, died in Guwahati on November 21, 2022, aged 12. His death marked the end of an extraordinary career that had taken him through some of Assam’s most important wildlife habitats. Yet, for the conservationists and handlers who worked alongside him, he was much more than a trained sniffer dog. He was a colleague, a companion and a conservation hero.How Zorba became Assam’s first anti-poaching dogZorba’s journey began in 2011, when biodiversity conservation organisation Aaranyak established a K9 unit in Assam to assist forest officials in tackling wildlife crime. He was the first dog inducted into the squad and was deployed in Kaziranga, where rhino poaching had become a serious conservation concern. The challenge for forest personnel was not limited to catching poachers at the scene. Suspects frequently escaped into the dense vegetation, leaving officials with little evidence beyond footprints, discarded objects or other traces of their presence. Zorba brought an important new ability to these investigations: his extraordinary sense of smell.A 2018 report by Mongabay, which documented his work in Kaziranga, described how the Belgian Malinois was trained to follow scents and locate people hiding in the forest. His handler, Goura Baidya, was particularly impressed by his determination once he picked up a trail. “Once set tracking, after made to sniff a scent, he is simply unstoppable, no matter what comes his way,” Baidya told Mongabay.The partnership between the dog and his handler became an important part of the K9 unit's work. Zorba was not simply sent into the forest to search independently; he worked alongside trained personnel who interpreted his signals and helped turn his tracking abilities into actionable evidence.The camera trap he pulled out of a pondAmong Zorba’s most remarkable operations was an investigation in which he helped recover a camera trap from a pond. The device had photographs of poachers in action, making it an important piece of evidence for investigators. Finding the camera was no ordinary task. It required Zorba to identify and follow a scent trail, eventually locating an object that might otherwise have remained undiscovered. The recovered photographs helped authorities identify those involved and make arrests.In another operation, the dog followed a blood trail left by an injured poacher for nearly 1.5 km. His ability to stay on the trail helped forest officials locate the suspect, demonstrating how a dog's sense of smell could make a difference in difficult investigations across the forest.His contribution was not restricted to Kaziranga either. Zorba was also deployed in other protected areas, including Orang National Park and Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary. In one incident in Orang, he followed a suspect's scent from the crime scene to a house outside the park. The clues he provided helped authorities identify the residence and arrest the accused.More than 60 poachers tracked during his careerBy 2018, Zorba had assisted in 18 successful operations and was credited with helping secure nearly 30 arrests, according to Mongabay's report. The figure increased over the following years. By August 2022, reports citing Aaranyak credited him with helping law enforcement agencies track down more than 60 poachers, including around 50 in Kaziranga. His contribution also helped establish the importance of trained dogs in wildlife crime investigations.What began with one Belgian Malinois gradually developed into a larger K9 unit. By August 2022, the squad had seven dogs, with two more undergoing training, according to a PTI report. The dogs assisted forest and police personnel in tracking suspects, identifying escape routes and locating evidence following poaching incidents. Aaranyak's initiative demonstrated how canine units could strengthen conservation efforts, particularly in areas where following human tracks through difficult terrain was challenging.Dr Bibhab Kumar Talukdar, Aaranyak's secretary general and chief executive, described Zorba as a conservation hero. His contribution, Talukdar said, would always be remembered.A ball-loving dog who became a conservation heroFor all his determination during operations, Zorba also had a playful side. His handlers remembered him not only for the trails he followed but also for the simple things he enjoyed. A report on his death quoted a member of the K9 unit recalling Zorba's particular fondness for playing with balls. The handler said that beyond their professional relationship, he would miss playing with the dog.Another handler, Mrigen Das, spoke of his special affection for Zorba because of the work the canine had done. His first handler, Anil Kumar Das, also remembered him as an inspiration and said he had immensely rich memories with him.After being relieved of active duty in December 2019, Zorba remained at Aaranyak's K9 unit centre. In August 2022, he was honoured for his service with a traditional Assamese gamosa and a citation on Independence Day.He died in Guwahati on November 21, 2022, following age-related health problems. His passing was mourned by wildlife conservationists and those who had worked with him. Aaranyak remembered him as one of the most important members of its wildlife protection efforts.
