articles.title: Scientists discover a new deep-sea species in Japanese underwater caves that flashes green light when disturbed, with its glow peaking at 515.4 nanometres
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a new deep-sea species that flashes green light when disturbed inside underwater caves near Japan.
articles.body: Scientists have discovered a new deep-sea species that flashes green light when disturbed inside underwater caves near Japan. Named Corallizoanthus aureus, the marine animal was found living on colonies of Pleurocorallium coral near the entrances of karst caves around Minamidaito Island. Researchers recorded its blinking light after mechanical and chemical stimulation, including during observations inside the cave.The glow had a measured peak wavelength of 515.4 ± 5.1 nanometres. According to research published in Royal Society Open Science titled ‘Glow in the D-ARK: a new bioluminescent species of Corallizoanthus from southern Japan’, the discovery provides the first documented observation of bioluminescence inside a deep-sea cave. The researchers said the light may serve a defensive role, although its exact ecological function remains unknown.A golden-coloured species discovered in deep-sea coral coloniesThe researchers found Corallizoanthus aureus during deep-sea surveys around Minamidaito Island in southern Japan. The island lies about 360 kilometres west of Okinawa-jima Island and has steep, complex and difficult-to-reach underwater terrain. The team discovered the species living on colonies of Pleurocorallium coral at the entrances of several karst caves.It was formally described as a new species after researchers combined morphological, genetic, and molecular evidence. The species name aureus comes from the Latin word for golden. Its living polyps, including their distinctive tentacles and oral discs, are bright yellow. The researchers collected specimens from a depth of 385 metres in May 2024 and July 2025.Deep-sea tests reveal the species’ ability to produce blinking green lightResearchers used remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) to explore the underwater caves as part of the international Deep-sea Archaic Refugia in Karst research project surveys. The team used the ROV KM-ROV with an attached sampling vehicle, TriPodFinder2. They tested the animals’ ability to produce light after collecting specimens.In a dark room aboard the research vessel at sea, they pinched the polyps with forceps and added potassium chloride to seawater containing the specimens. The team also tested living polyps inside the cave by mechanically stimulating them with a suction sampler during the research dives. In both settings, the polyps produced blinking green light after the team applied the stimulation.What causes the deep-sea animal to produce green lightThe light came from the polyps rather than the thin connections, known as stolons, linking some of them. Researchers measured the glow’s spectral peak at 515.4 ± 5.1 nanometres, with results from four replicates. During a separate underwater observation, the light appeared to spread visibly from the area where the animal was stimulated.The researchers did not observe any spontaneous light production during the reported study. They also found no sign of symbiotic bacteria in tissue examinations of Corallizoanthus aureus. Based on existing knowledge, they suggested that the animal’s light may involve the molecule coelenterazine and an unidentified light-producing enzyme called luciferase.Scientists suggest green flashes may help the animal defend itself against predatorsThe ecological purpose of this green glow is not yet known. The researchers suggested that it may have a defensive role and discussed a possible ‘burglar alarm’ effect. Under this explanation, light produced by prey could attract larger predators that attack the animal’s immediate predator. Another possibility is a luminous tag.Sticky glowing mucus or detached body parts could remain on a predator, making it visible and more vulnerable to larger hunters. These two ideas remain possible explanations rather than established functions of the species’ light. The researchers said further field observations and detailed studies are needed in the future to understand how bioluminescence works in this group and what role it plays in the deep-sea cave environment around Minamidaito Island.

articles.title: A 3,800-year-old woman once wrote a frustrated letter to her husband complaining about a debtor who refused to repay him; archaeologists have now read the ancient message without breaking its clay envelope
articles.summary: The struggle to recover money someone owes you is familiar, even if the person on the other end of the transaction lived thousands of years ago.
articles.body: The struggle to recover money someone owes you is familiar, even if the person on the other end of the transaction lived thousands of years ago. Imagine the disappointment of a woman instructed by her husband to retrieve silver he was owed, who, upon failure, penned her frustration in a letter addressed to him.For Anna-anna, who lived nearly 4,000 years ago in ancient Anatolia, this was precisely what happened. She wrote to her husband, Ennum-Aššur, a merchant who travelled across cities for business in central Anatolia. The message, etched on a cuneiform tablet, was brought to light by researchers at the Centre for the Study of Manuscript Cultures at the University of Hamburg. But perhaps an even more intriguing detail is that the researchers managed to discover the contents of the letter without ever opening the clay envelope that had protected it for millennia.In an article on the technology used to access the letter, the CSMC reported that, while Ennum-Aššur was conducting business in central Anatolia, he had asked his wife to recover silver he was owed by a fellow merchant, Laqēpum. However, when Anna-anna approached the debtor, he refused to hand over the silver to her, claiming that he would repay her husband personally upon his return. He also claimed to have paid the silver to another individual, Kudātum. Anna-anna then wrote a letter to Ennum-Aššur to inform him of what had happened, leaving behind a glimpse of an everyday disagreement and offering a look into how similar problems existed even thousands of years ago.The tablet containing the letter was discovered during excavations at Kültepe, the ancient settlement of Kanesh in present-day Türkiye, and is now preserved at the Museum of Anatolian Civilisations in Ankara. Although the names of the sender and intended recipient, Anna-anna and Ennum-Aššur, could be read on the envelope, the message itself remained inaccessible, enclosed within its original clay covering. The letter had remained unread for nearly 4,000 years, including possibly by Ennum-Aššur, to whom it was addressed. It is possible that the letter never reached her husband at all. While we do not know how the conversation would have unfolded had he received it, the fact that the letter has now been read while preserving the artefact itself is a remarkable achievement.Ancient writing system and how letters were protectedClay envelopes were used in ancient Mesopotamia to protect written messages from damage and keep their contents private while they travelled between the sender and recipient. The letters themselves were inscribed on clay tablets using cuneiform, an indispensable writing system used across ancient Mesopotamia and other regions. Using wedge-shaped impressions, scribes inscribed their messages into the clay. The tablets could then be enclosed within another layer of clay bearing the names of the sender and recipient, along with impressions of their seals.For archaeologists, however, the task at hand was not simple. They could not read the letter without risking damage to its envelope, which was itself a valuable historical artefact. Although archaeological science has witnessed remarkable advances in examining ancient objects, the ideal technology for this task was X-ray microtomography, which produces detailed three-dimensional images of an artifact's internal structure. Conventional tomographic scanners, however, can be extremely large and heavy, making them difficult to transport. Since the letter was housed in a museum, moving it to a specialised laboratory for scanning was not an ideal solution.A unique way of accessing historyThis is where ENCI, short for Extracting Non-destructively Cuneiform Inscriptions, entered the picture. According to an article in npj Heritage Science, ENCI was developed by an interdisciplinary team involving researchers from the University of Hamburg and the German research institution DESY. This mobile computed tomography scanner uses X-rays to examine sealed clay objects without opening them.The team brought together specialists from different fields, including Assyriologist Cécile Michel, X-ray physicist Christian Schroer and computer scientist Stephan Olbrich. Through this multidisciplinary approach, the researchers were able to collect and process tomographic data, reconstruct the tablet's internal structure and visualise its inscriptions. This allowed them to access the contents of the letter without physically opening the envelope.However, ENCI is not limited to only clay tablets; the researchers have also demonstrated its use on other cultural heritage objects, including a ninth-century Georgian codex, Egyptian statuettes and Mesopotamian cylinder seals.This portable invention simplifies a fairly arduous task for experts, making the science of decoding easier. An ordinary conversation, a simple negotiation, gave light to a familial life. While both the wife and husband are known only through this letter, the move towards a mobile CT scanner has wonderfully tapped into the history preserved within material cultures, although only figuratively.

articles.title: A teenager tending livestock near the Dead Sea threw a stone into a cave and heard something shatter; the accidental discovery eventually led researchers to the Dead Sea Scrolls, among the most important ancient manuscripts ever found
articles.summary: Some incredible findings emerge from happy accidents.
articles.body: Some incredible findings emerge from happy accidents. In 1947, a young Bedouin shepherd searching for a stray animal near the Dead Sea threw a stone into a cave and heard the sound of pottery breaking. This led to the discovery of a collection of ancient manuscripts hidden for centuries, finally giving researchers a glimpse into the religious life and history preserved in the scrolls.The shepherd, commonly identified as Mohammed edh-Dhib, was searching among the rocky cliffs of the Judean Desert near the site of Qumran when he came across the cave. According to the widely recounted account of this encounter, the sound of the stone striking a pottery jar made him curious. According to the Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library and the Israel Antiquities Authority, the manuscripts discovered in the cave eventually became known as the Dead Sea Scrolls, marking the beginning of one of the most significant archaeological discoveries of the 20th century.A discovery that went beyond seven scrollsThe first cave yielded seven scrolls, or nearly complete manuscripts, which eventually came to the attention of scholars. Initially, the objects passed through local hands before their historical significance was recognised. The location and naming of these scrolls carry a history of their own. Located about 15 miles east of Jerusalem, regarded as the holiest city in Judaism, the site is also associated with an important period in biblical history.Between 1947 and 1956, researchers discovered manuscripts and fragments in 11 caves in the area. According to the Library of Congress, these discoveries yielded thousands of fragments, revealing not only the contents of the manuscripts but also details about their materials and production. The Psalms Scroll, found in Cave 11 in 1956 and unrolled in 1961, is made from particularly thick parchment. Its surface suggests that it may have been made from calfskin rather than sheepskin, which was more commonly used as writing material at Qumran. This accidental discovery has provided generations of researchers, archaeologists and historians with insights into material culture that are still being explored today.The manuscripts were primarily written in Hebrew, although some were in Aramaic and Greek. They included copies of biblical books, prayers, hymns, religious interpretations and other writings associated with Jewish communities of the period. Some of the texts are among the oldest surviving manuscript copies of books that later formed part of the Hebrew Bible. For researchers, this led to an examination of how religious texts were copied, preserved and understood long before the surviving medieval manuscripts that provided much of the earlier evidence.What the manuscripts reveal about the ancient worldThe Dead Sea Scrolls are generally dated between the third century BCE and the first century CE, placing them within the Second Temple period in Jewish history. Their contents provide insight into the religious ideas, practices and disagreements that existed during this time, when Jewish communities were far from uniform in their beliefs and interpretations.The significance of the scrolls extends beyond the study of religious texts themselves. They have helped scholars examine the development of biblical literature and the historical setting in which early Christianity emerged. Rather than providing details about a particular historical incident, the scrolls offer evidence of the diverse religious writings, beliefs and practices that existed during this period.The caves also raised questions about the people who placed the manuscripts there and the circumstances of their deposit. Archaeologist Roland de Vaux, who excavated the nearby settlement of Qumran, associated the site with a Jewish religious community often identified as the Essenes. However, the precise relationship between the settlement, the caves and the different groups that may have produced or collected the texts remains a subject of archaeological discussion.How the desert preserved a forgotten collectionAnother remarkable aspect of the discovery is that the manuscripts survived for nearly two millennia. The dry conditions of the Judean Desert helped preserve materials such as parchment and papyrus, although not all the scrolls survived in the same condition. Many were recovered only as fragments, leading to painstaking examination as researchers pieced together different sections to interpret them as a whole.Sites near the Dead Sea include Masada, Ein Gedi and Qumran. Alongside the discoveries at Qumran, Masada and other locations in the region have also yielded ancient manuscripts and fragments. The Dead Sea Scrolls were formerly exhibited by the Library of Congress in 1993, bringing their historical and archaeological significance to a wider audience. However, some of the most important evidence from these scrolls lies not only in their contents but also in the materials used to create them. A mere happy accident has today provided insights into not only what was written nearly 2,000 years ago but perhaps also an understanding of the local arts, communities and crafts that came together in the making of these manuscripts.

articles.title: Musk makes light of defeats after record spend on Republican candidates
articles.summary: Tesla and SpaceX founder Elon Musk is the world’s richest man and the largest individual donor in the US midterms.
articles.body:
Elon Musk has joked online about the Republican defeat in the US midterm elections after spending nearly half a billion dollars to bolster the party’s campaigns.

Republicans were decisively routed by Democrats in Tuesday’s polls, losing control of the Senate and the House of Representatives, while racking up losses in states long seen as Republican strongholds, such as Texas and Kansas.

“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” the Tesla and SpaceX founder wrote on X, which he owns, on Wednesday.

Musk reportedly spent $446m supporting Republican candidates in the elections, making him the top donor.

His donations have mostly gone to his own Republican-leaning political action committee, America PAC, and to the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) super PAC.

The SLF used Musk’s $158m in donations in September to support Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas, who lost to Democrat James Talarico.

Voters rejected Paxton’s plan to make Texas the centre of the country’s artificial intelligence (AI) industry by rapidly building data centres. Talarico campaigned for tighter regulations on their development.

Musk took to X to joke: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now”.

The South Africa-born entrepreneur has moved the headquarters of his companies Tesla, SpaceX, and X to Texas.

Talarico explicitly referenced Musk in his election victory speech, saying his campaign had taken on “goliaths” including “the richest man in the world” and won.

Musk, who became a trillionaire in June when his company SpaceX went public, supported the Republican campaign for governor of Texas, a race which the Democrats also won.

Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Governor Greg Abbott despite a $5m donation by Musk to the Republican candidate.

Huge campaign donations by billionaires have become part of the political reality in the US since a 2010 Supreme Court ruling that the government could not limit political spending by corporations, unions, and other groups if they spend it independently of candidates.

articles.title: SpaceX inks Qualcomm deal, putting Starlink closer to becoming the fourth major US wireless carrier
articles.summary: SpaceX is teaming with Qualcomm in push to turn Starlink into major US carrier.
articles.body:
SpaceX's ( SPCX ) goal of turning its Starlink service into a major US mobile carrier is one step closer to becoming a reality.

On Wednesday, Qualcomm ( QCOM ) announced that SpaceX has selected its Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure platforms to power Starlink Mobile's nationwide terrestrial 5G cellular network.

Starlink already has the largest satellite-based network, and the ground-based stations will allow it to better compete with AT&T ( T ), T-Mobile ( TMUS ), and Verizon ( VZ ).

Last month, the company announced an agreement to purchase licenses for 800 MHz spectrum.

"While Starlink Mobile's global 2 GHz mid-band spectrum will provide high-bandwidth capacity in the United States, this new low-band spectrum will provide a coverage layer that ensures Starlink Mobile's signal penetrates through obstacles, such as walls, and can provide service to customers' devices even when they are in buildings," the company said at the time.

According to Qualcomm, the new deal will allow both companies to begin deploying advanced 5G service and provide "an opportunity to lay the foundation for AI-native 6G in the years ahead."

The company says the effort will require SpaceX to deploy its chip technology across tens of thousands of cellular towers nationwide.

"Our agreement with SpaceX is structured in such a way that as the deployment begins, starting from next year, it's going to ramp up pretty rapidly from there onwards," said Durga Malladi, EVP and GM for technology planning, edge solutions, and data center at Qualcomm.

"So it's a multi-year agreement that we have with them in terms of the deployment capability as we ramp up all the way to nationwide coverage," he added.

Earlier this month, The Washington Post reported that SpaceX was in talks with EchoStar ( ECHO ) to operate its own carrier through EchoStar's Boost Mobile brand.

The company made the move after AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon reportedly rejected its requests to use their network capacity through a mobile virtual network operator (MVNO) deal.

An MVNO rents capacity from existing carriers and sells it under its own branding. But an operator like Starlink Mobile could prove a particularly potent challenger to the Big Three network carriers, leaving them little incentive to work with Elon Musk's firm.

articles.title: Elon Musk's millions fail to deliver Texas for the Republicans
articles.summary: The billionaire's political action committee (Pac) contributed $47m (£35m) to Ken Paxton's campaign.
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico's resounding victory in the Texas Senate race caused a major upset in the midterms for Republicans - and for Elon Musk.

According to the Financial Times , the billionaire's political action committee (Pac) contributed $47m (£35m) to Republican candidate Ken Paxton's campaign, on top of the $158m he gave the Senate Leadership Fund in September.

The money was not enough to stop the seat from turning Democrat for the first time since 1988. In his acceptance speech, Talarico said: "We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas."

"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," Musk jokingly wrote on X .

While stocks were broadly up on Wednesday morning following the election outcome, Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were down by 4.9% and 3.4% respectively. Many Democrats had been vocally outspoken against the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres on the campaign trail.

Democrats take control of US Congress as voters resoundingly reject Trump's Republicans

Talarico's victory marked a key turning point in the midterms, helping solidify the Democrats' control of the US Congress in a wave of wins across the US .

Musk has increasingly made Texas the hub of his companies, from Tesla's Austin headquarters to SpaceX's Starbase launch site.

As well as backing Paxton through outside groups, the X owner took to his own platform to spread conspiracy theories about the Democrat, posting: "There is something deeply wrong with Talarico" after he briefly disappeared from the campaign trail in October.

"There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator," Talarico posted in response.

On top of contributing to one of the most expensive Senate races ever, the SpaceX owner also became the top individual donor in this year's midterms overall , contributing an estimated $446m in backing Republican candidates.

Musk's money went through Super Pacs, groups which can raise unlimited sums but can't give directly to candidates or coordinate with their campaigns.

Individuals, parties and traditional groups face legal limits on direct donations.

Super Pacs get around this by spending independently, such as on ads backing a candidate.

Musk became one of the Republican Party's biggest donors in 2024, pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Donald Trump's winning presidential campaign.

A similarly eye-watering amount was not enough to do the same for Paxton this time around.

articles.body: SpaceX is teaming up with Qualcomm to build out its nationwide mobile network. Under the multi-year deal, SpaceX will bring Qualcomm’s Dragonwing technology to “tens of thousands” of 5G cell sites across the US, with the first deployments set for 2027. The news of the partnership comes as part of SpaceX’s push to make Starlink Mobile a “major” carrier in the US, competing directly with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon. The Elon Musk-owned company has already snapped up a swath of spectrum, while recent reports suggested that SpaceX was exploring an acquisition of Boost Mobile. Now, SpaceX is planning to use Qualcomm’s Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure, a platform made up of hardware and software designed to boost network coverage, capacity, and efficiency. SpaceX plans to combine this infrastructure with its constellation of direct-to-cell satellites. “Together with SpaceX, we are building world-leading cellular infrastructure in the United States, advancing 5G today,” Durga Malladi, Qualcomm’s executive vice president and general manager of technology planning, edge solutions, and data center, says. He adds that the companies have the opportunity to “lay the foundation” for 6G in the coming years.

articles.title: A 3,200-pound NASA observatory plunged back to Earth. Here’s what to know
articles.summary: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory fell to a fiery end early Wednesday nearly 22 years after it launched.
articles.body:
NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory met a fiery end on Wednesday morning, nearly 22 years after it launched to study the most powerful explosions in the universe.

Data from the US Space Force estimates the 3,200-pound spacecraft plunged into Earth's atmosphere over Indonesia around 7:39 a.m. ET.

While most of the observatory was expected to burn up as it blazed through the thick inner band of Earth's atmosphere, NASA predicted some pieces of the vehicle would survive.

It was not immediately clear whether any surviving debris hit land. Previously, NASA had predicted that the "risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely, approximately 1 in 2,100."

If Swift were launched today, it would likely have to adhere to far stricter safety guidelines regarding end-of-life planning, according to The Aerospace Corporation, which is a federally funded research and development center.

Current orbital debris mitigation standards , which were updated in 2019, mandate that "uncontrolled reentries have an expected casualty of less than 1 in 10,000," said Parker Wishik, a spokesperson for The Aerospace Corporation. He noted in an email that, in this context, "casualty" refers to "serious injury or death."

While NASA has long known that Swift would likely have to make an unpredictable plunge back to Earth, the agency had hoped that a daring rescue mission launched in July could latch on and boost the Swift Observatory as atmospheric drag gradually pulled it from a once-stable orbit. It could have extended Swift's operating life by a decade or more, but ultimately the effort failed. The spacecraft eventually dropped down to just 171 miles (275 kilometers) above the planet, and the observatory officially stopped gathering scientific data.

"At this point, the spacecraft was no longer able to compensate for the effects of the increased drag and entered safe mode," NASA said in a news release .

A team of researchers at Penn State — NASA's partner on the project and home to the observatory's Mission Operations Center — sent the final kill-switch command to Swift on October 20.

Swift's demise was hastened by an increase in solar activity over the past couple of years as the sun reached the peak of its 11-year cycle in 2024.

Intense flares and coronal mass ejections caused Earth's atmosphere to expand, which intensified the drag on Swift, leading scientists to predict it would descend toward our planet this fall.

Arizona-based Katalyst Space Technologies scrambled to put together the last-ditch effort to stabilize the Swift observatory earlier this year, getting the rescue mission off the ground in only nine months. The company rapidly produced a spacecraft called LINK, which aimed to grapple the telescope and lift it back into a stable orbit. But the mission failed a few weeks after LINK's launch in July as the satellite spun out of control in space before reaching the Swift observatory.

As Swift's fate was sealed, mission scientists slowly turned the telescope's instruments back on to collect data and observations right up until the end. The instruments had been shut off for months to save power and mitigate how quickly the spacecraft sank out of orbit.

The Swift Observatory, which does not have an established observational replacement waiting in the wings, has served as an astrophysics multi-tool in low-Earth orbit since it launched in November 2004.

Named after fast-flying birds, the telescope could quickly pivot to observe blink-and-you-miss-it cosmic events such as flaring black holes. The telescope was originally designed to study the most powerful explosions in the universe, called gamma-ray bursts, but scientists have also used it to monitor other types of cosmic flashes as well as asteroids and comets.

Despite the failed attempt to rescue Swift, NASA has signaled it may try similar lifeline-extension missions for other valuable space-based instruments. Last week, the agency issued a solicitation — formally called a Request for Proposals or RFP — to commercial companies, asking how they might boost, service or otherwise prolong the life of the iconic Hubble Space Telescope.

NASA's analysis shows that there's a 10% chance Hubble will plunge out of orbit by 2032 and a 50% it will deorbit by 2033, according to the RFP. The beloved telescope, launched in 1990, has delivered some of the most recognizable images in astronomy and has transformed scientists' understanding of the cosmos. There is no replacement for Hubble expected before the 2040s, the RFP states.

articles.title: NASA space telescope plunges to Earth after two decades studying cosmic explosions
articles.summary: One of NASA’s premier space telescopes plunged to Earth on Wednesday, ending its 22-year investigation of the universe’s biggest explosions.
articles.body: One of NASA’s premier space telescopes plunged to Earth on Wednesday, ending its 22-year investigation of the universe’s biggest explosions. The Swift Observatory’s demise came less than three months after a long-shot rescue mission failed. The U.S. Space Force confirmed Swift’s reentry near Indonesia after tracking its sinking orbit, the result of intense solar activity the past few years. NASA hired a private company to whip together an orbit-boosting effort, but Katalyst Space's three-armed robotic craft ran into trouble following its July launch and came crashing down in September. It was not immediately known how much of the 1 ½-ton spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere. NASA anticipated some of the denser pieces surviving. Swift rocketed into orbit in 2004 on what was expected to be a two-year study of gamma ray bursts and exploding stars. It observed thousands of them over a mission that lasted 11 times longer than planned, serving as a first responder for other telescopes that could probe deeper. NASA is gauging industry’s interest in mounting a rescue mission for another observatory whose orbit is being chipped away by solar storms: the Hubble Space Telescope. Launched in 1990, Hubble is expected to come crashing down by the mid-2030s, according to recent analyses. The space agency is looking for input from private companies on whether and how they might boost Hubble’s orbit, upgrade its systems or guide it to a controlled reentry — or all three. Any such mission would need to happen by 2032. Unlike the rush job with Swift, the space agency has more time to explore options for saving Hubble, said Nicky Fox, NASA’s science mission chief. “Hubble still has important science ahead of it,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement, “and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible.”

articles.title: 17 better ways Elon Musk could have wasted $446 million
articles.summary: Elon Musk flushed about half a billion down the toilet on the midterms. He could have gotten his own film version of The Odyssey off the ground with that budget.
articles.body: One of the basic problems of spending too much time on social media is that you are cooking your brain by reading posts from a pack of attention-seeking lunatics. If your social media of choice is the site formerly known as Twitter, and it is your main source of contact with the outside world, you may delusionally throw away nearly $500 million dollars on midterm elections, just like Elon Musk. In particular, $47 million of that money from Musk’s America PAC was aimed at defeating Texas Democrat James Talarico, who trounced Musk’s preferred Senate candidate, Ken Paxton, with 55 percent of the vote. Talarico even made Musk’s influence a central part of his campaign ads, with the slogan “Texas is not for sale.” How did Musk get this so wrong? I blame the bubble of X. My former colleague Casey Newton, who has (with some well-earned shame) slunk back to X, explained that he did so because it was the site that was most influential with the AI crowd. In some sense, this is exactly the problem. The agentmaxxing loons of AI influencing are wildly out of touch with normal people. There is, right now, one very important bipartisan position in the United States, and it is: Fuck a data center. It’s pretty obvious that the opposition to data centers is a way of making concrete how pissed off most people are with the tech industry, particularly with the gangster tech regulation of late and the constant stream of threats coming from AI companies. These guys have really tied themselves and their AI aspirations to Donald Trump’s sinking ship, and if you’re hanging out on X all the time, that’s impossible to see, not least because the site’s owner, Musk, is shaping the algorithm in ways that make him feel good. Since Musk seems to have forgotten what it is like to experience joy, or even mild satisfaction, I have taken the liberty to make a list of things he could have bought to get him a better return on his investment. He probably could flip several things on this list for more money, but at minimum he could have gotten a little rush of pleasure from a new purchase: * Larry Ellison’s private island ($300 million in 2012, $440 million in today’s dollars per CPI calculator) (source) * 13 Rolls-Royce La Rose Noire Droptails ($32 million) (source) * 5 The Graff Diamonds Hallucination watches ($55 million, $78 million today) (source) * The Washington Post ($250 million in 2013, $360 million today) (source) * 30 Sunseeker 100 yachts (base price $14.6 million) (source) * 43 Hope diamonds ($300,000 in 1911, about $10.3 million today) (source) * Ken Griffin’s NYC penthouse ($239.96 million in 2019, $321 million today) (source) * 76 New Zealand golden visas ($10 million plus $27,000 application fee in NZD, about $5.77 million in USD) (source) * 44 30-second Super Bowl commercials ($10 million) (source) * At least 977 rides on Blue Origin’s New Shepard ($450,000) (source) * Willem de Kooning’s Interchange (~$300 million, ~$400 million today) (source) * $14.67 gift card to every Texan (~30 million Texans) (source) * 34 renovations of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool ($13.1 million) (source) * 223,000 Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards (at MSRP of $1,999) (source); 60,000 Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards (at “globalized normal price” of $7,240) (source) * 8 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show Fantasy Bras (source) * His very own non-Grok version of The Odyssey (budget $250 million) (source) * 4 sets of Wachtell, Lipton lawyers from the Twitter takeover suit ($90 million fee) (source) But hey, at least changing the name of SpaceX’s “Superintelligence” division back to “Artificial Intelligence” is free! Musk spent last night deleting tweets so he wouldn’t look as stupid as he is. Too bad it’s not as easy to delete other things! Texans were already asking questions about sweetheart deals to benefit Musk, and now there’s a wave of politicians who ran against his money coming into power, including the governor and the attorney general of Texas. That may mean unredacting Gov. Greg Abbott’s Musk emails, for instance — answering some questions about the influence Musk bought with Texas Republicans. So actually, maybe the best investment on that list would be the dream team of lawyers who clobbered Musk on the Twitter deal — because Musk has a bunch of new enemies in power, and the simplest thing in the world they can do to curry favor with their voters is investigate him. Bet you’d never know that if you spent all your time on X.
